title: Arrays & contiguous memory
hook: An array is just items laid out back-to-back — so index math can jump straight to a slot.

steps.caption: You ask for index 2. No walking — start address + 2 × item size lands on the slot.

nodeCaptions.index: Random access: time doesn’t grow with how far the index is.
nodeCaptions.s2: Contiguous layout is what makes the jump possible.

steps.caption: The value comes straight back. Slots 0 and 1 weren’t visited.

nodeCaptions.s0: Still there — just not needed for this lookup.
nodeCaptions.s1: Arrays trade flexible insert/delete for O(1) reads by index.

takeaways: Contiguous memory + fixed item size ⇒ direct index addressing.
Reading by index is fast; inserting in the middle usually means shifting neighbors.
Cache-friendly layouts matter because CPUs love sequential memory.

quiz.question: Why can an array jump to index 100 without visiting 0–99?
choices: It stores a pointer to every index in a hash map
Items sit in contiguous memory, so address = start + index × size
Arrays are stored on disk only
quiz.explanation: That’s the whole point of contiguous layout.
